title: The Elevator
situation: A man lives on the 20th floor of an apartment building. Every morning he takes the elevator down to the ground floor and goes to work. In the evening, he takes the elevator to the 10th floor and walks up the stairs the rest of the way, unless it is raining or someone else is in the elevator. Why?
solution: The man is very short. He can only reach the button for the 10th floor. On rainy days he has an umbrella and uses it to press the 20th-floor button, and when someone else is in the elevator he asks them to press it.
keyFacts: The man is short (a person of small stature)
He cannot reach the higher buttons
The umbrella lets him press the button on rainy days
hints: Think about what is physically different between the morning trip and the evening trip.
The rain itself is not the reason. What does a person carry when it rains?
Something about the man himself prevents him from going straight to the 20th floor.

title: A Glass of Water
situation: A man walks into a bar and asks the bartender for a glass of water. The bartender pulls out a gun and points it at the man. The man says 'thank you' and leaves. Why?
solution: The man had hiccups. The bartender realised this and scared him with the gun. The fright cured the hiccups, so the man no longer needed the water and thanked the bartender.
keyFacts: The man had hiccups
The gun was meant to scare him
The fright cured the hiccups
hints: The man was not in any danger and the bartender was being helpful.
Why would someone want a glass of water other than thirst?
A sudden shock can cure a common, harmless condition.

title: Romeo and Juliet
situation: Romeo and Juliet are found dead on the floor of a room. Around them are broken glass and a puddle of water. There are no marks on their bodies. What happened?
solution: Romeo and Juliet are goldfish. Their bowl was knocked off a table (by a cat, a gust of wind, or similar) and shattered, and they died on the floor.
keyFacts: Romeo and Juliet are fish (goldfish)
Their bowl fell and broke
hints: Romeo and Juliet are not human.
Think about what the water and glass were before they ended up on the floor.
They lived in the water.

title: The Unopened Package
situation: A man is lying dead in a field. Next to him is an unopened package. There is no one else around. How did he die?
solution: The man jumped from a plane and his parachute failed to open. The unopened package is the parachute.
keyFacts: He fell from a great height (jumped from a plane)
The package is a parachute that did not open
hints: The package is directly connected to his death.
If the package had been opened, he would have lived.
He arrived in the field from above.

title: The Cabin
situation: Two people are found dead inside a cabin on the side of a mountain. The cabin is intact and locked from the inside. There is no sign of violence and no one else is around. How did they die?
solution: The cabin is the cabin of an aeroplane that crashed into the mountain. The two people were the pilots (or passengers) who died in the crash.
keyFacts: The cabin is an aircraft cabin
The plane crashed into the mountain
hints: It is not a log cabin.
The cabin did not start out on the mountain.
Think about other things that have a 'cabin'.

title: When the Music Stopped
situation: The music stopped. She died. Explain.
solution: She was a blindfolded tightrope walker in a circus. The band's music was her cue: as long as it played, she knew she had not yet reached the end of the rope. When the music stopped early, she thought she had reached the platform, stepped off, and fell to her death.
keyFacts: She was a tightrope walker / performing at height
She was blindfolded (or otherwise relied on the music for timing)
The music stopping made her step off and fall
hints: She was a performer.
She could not see where she was going.
The music told her something about her position.

title: The Man with the Straw
situation: A man is found dead in the desert, naked, holding half a straw. How did he die?
solution: He was in a hot-air balloon with companions. The balloon was losing altitude, so they threw out everything they could, including their clothes. It was still sinking, so they drew straws to decide who would jump. He drew the short straw and jumped to his death.
keyFacts: He was in a hot-air balloon that was losing height
They threw everything overboard, including clothes
They drew straws and he lost, so he jumped
hints: He was not alone when he died.
He and his companions were in the air.
The straw was part of a decision-making process.

title: Albatross Soup
situation: A man walks into a restaurant by the sea and orders albatross soup. He takes one spoonful, puts the spoon down, walks out, and shoots himself. Why?
solution: Years earlier, he had been shipwrecked with his wife and other survivors. They were starving. The other survivors told him his wife had died and gave him what they said was albatross meat to eat. Tasting real albatross soup, he realised that what he had eaten back then was not albatross: it was his wife. Overcome with horror, he killed himself.
keyFacts: He had been shipwrecked / starving earlier in life
He had been fed something he was told was albatross
The taste revealed it was not albatross; he had eaten his wife (a human)
hints: The taste of the soup triggered a memory.
He had eaten 'albatross' once before, under extreme circumstances.
Whatever he ate back then was not really albatross.

title: Dinner After the Shooting
situation: A woman shoots her husband. Then she holds him under water for several minutes. Finally she hangs him. Shortly afterwards they go out together and enjoy a lovely dinner. How is this possible?
solution: The woman is a photographer. She shot a photo of her husband, developed it in a water bath, and hung it up to dry.
keyFacts: She 'shot' him with a camera (took a photograph)
The water and the hanging refer to developing and drying the photo
hints: No one was hurt.
'Shoot' has more than one meaning.
The water and the hanging were part of a process, not an attack.

title: The Hotel
situation: A man pushes his car up to a hotel and immediately knows he is bankrupt. Why?
solution: He is playing Monopoly. His playing piece is the car, and he has landed on a property with a hotel on it that he cannot afford.
keyFacts: He is playing a board game (Monopoly)
The car is his playing piece
Landing on the hotel means paying rent he cannot afford
hints: The car is very small.
There are other people playing with him.
The hotel belongs to one of them.

title: The Locked Room
situation: A man is found hanged in a locked room. The room is completely empty except for a puddle of water beneath his feet. There is nothing he could have stood on. How did he do it?
solution: He stood on a large block of ice to reach the noose. The ice melted, leaving only the puddle.
keyFacts: He stood on a block of ice
The ice melted, leaving the puddle
hints: The puddle is the key clue.
Something that was there is no longer there.
What solid object turns into water?

title: The Poisoned Punch
situation: Two friends order the same drink at a bar. One drinks hers quickly and leaves. The other drinks his slowly, and dies. Both drinks were poisoned. Why did only one die?
solution: The poison was in the ice cubes. The woman drank quickly, before the ice melted. The man drank slowly, so the ice melted into his drink and he swallowed the poison.
keyFacts: The poison was in the ice
Drinking slowly let the ice melt and release the poison
hints: The drinks were identical at the start.
Time made the difference.
Not every part of the drink is liquid when it is served.

title: Lights Out
situation: A man turns off a light, goes to bed, and in the morning learns that many people have died because of what he did. Who is he?
solution: He is a lighthouse keeper. He switched off the lighthouse lamp, and during the night a ship struck the rocks and many people drowned.
keyFacts: He is a lighthouse keeper
Turning off the light caused a ship to wreck
hints: The light was not in his home.
The people who died were on the water.
His job was to keep that light on.

title: Carrot and Coal
situation: A carrot, two pieces of coal, and a scarf are lying on a lawn. Nobody put them there, yet there is a perfectly good reason for them to be there. What is it?
solution: They are the remains of a snowman that has melted.
keyFacts: They were parts of a snowman
The snowman melted
hints: Think about the season and the weather.
They were once arranged in a shape.
Something large was holding them and is now gone.

title: Not Twins
situation: Two children were born to the same mother, on the same day, at the same hour, in the same year, yet they are not twins. How?
solution: They are two of a set of triplets (or quadruplets).
keyFacts: They are part of a set of three or more (triplets)
hints: They are siblings.
They did share a birth.
How many children were born that day?

title: The Explorer's Discovery
situation: An explorer finds two perfectly preserved bodies in a cave. He looks at them for a moment and declares with certainty: 'These are Adam and Eve.' How does he know?
solution: The bodies have no navels (belly buttons). Adam and Eve were never born from a mother, so they would have no umbilical cord scar.
keyFacts: The bodies have no navels / belly buttons
Adam and Eve were never born, so they had no umbilical cords
hints: The explorer noticed something missing on the bodies.
Think about how Adam and Eve came into being, compared with everyone else.
Every person born from a mother carries one small scar for life.

title: The Phone Booth
situation: A man is found dead inside a phone booth. The glass panels on both sides are shattered and his hands are cut and bloody. Outside the booth lies a fishing rod. What happened?
solution: He had just caught a huge fish and was phoning a friend to tell him about it. Spreading his arms wide to show how big the fish was, he smashed both hands through the glass panels, cut his wrists, and bled to death.
keyFacts: He was describing the size of a fish with his arms
His arms went through the glass and he bled to death
hints: He was excited about something when he died.
The fishing rod matters: what do people do after fishing?
How do people show the size of something with their hands?

title: The Fly in the Coffee
situation: A woman in a café finds a fly in her coffee and sends it back. The waiter returns with a fresh cup. After one sip she says angrily: 'This is the same cup, you just removed the fly!' She is right. How did she know?
solution: She had already put sugar in her coffee before noticing the fly. The 'new' coffee was sweet, so it had to be the same cup.
keyFacts: She had already added sugar (or something) to the first cup
The 'fresh' cup tasted of it, so it was the same coffee
hints: She did something to the coffee before she saw the fly.
The proof was in the taste.
A truly fresh cup would have tasted different.

title: The Package
situation: A man receives a parcel in the post. He opens it and finds a human arm inside. He examines it, nods, says 'That's fine', and buries it in the garden. Why?
solution: Years ago he and two friends were stranded (after a shipwreck or in the mountains) and starving. They agreed that each of them would cut off an arm to eat, in turn. The others gave up their arms, but the man was rescued before his turn came. He later kept the promise by having his own arm amputated and sent it to his friends as proof. The arm in the parcel is from one of the friends doing the same, proving the pact is now fully honoured.
keyFacts: The men had been stranded and starving together
They made a pact to each sacrifice an arm to eat
The arm is proof that the pact was honoured
hints: The man is not surprised by the arm; he was expecting something like it.
He shares a history with the person who sent it, involving extreme hunger.
A promise made long ago is being kept.

title: One Ring at Nine
situation: Every evening at exactly nine o'clock, a woman's phone rings once and then falls silent. She never picks up and never calls back, yet each time she smiles with relief. It is not a fault and not a scam. What is going on?
solution: Her son is working far away, where calls are expensive and the connection is poor. They agreed that every night at nine he would let her phone ring once and hang up before she answered. The single ring is a free, pre-arranged signal that means 'I'm safe and well', so there is no need for her to answer or call back.
keyFacts: The call is from a loved one who is far away
The single ring is a pre-arranged signal meaning 'I am fine'
Not answering is deliberate: hanging up before pickup keeps it free and no conversation is needed
hints: The ring itself is the whole message.
The caller is someone she loves, a long way from home, and calls cost money.
They agreed in advance: one ring at nine means 'I'm safe' and nothing more needs to be said.

title: The Younger Twin Was Born First
situation: Emma was born a few minutes before her twin brother Liam, and the whole family agrees she is the older one. Yet Liam's birth certificate shows an earlier time of birth than Emma's, and both certificates are completely accurate. How is this possible?
solution: The twins were born on the night daylight saving time ended. Emma was born at about 1:50 in the morning; a few minutes later the clocks went back from 2:00 to 1:00. Liam arrived after the change, so his official time of birth was recorded as about 1:10, earlier on paper than his older sister's.
keyFacts: The clocks were changed (daylight saving time ended) between the two births
The clocks went back by an hour, so the later birth got an earlier recorded time
Both certificates record the correct official time for that moment
hints: Nobody made a mistake, and no one is lying. Think about the clock rather than the babies.
Something happened to the official time between the first birth and the second.
They were born on the night the clocks went back an hour.

title: The Frozen Orchard
situation: On the coldest night of spring, a fruit farmer switches on the sprinklers over her orchard and leaves them running all night, until every blossom is sealed inside a coat of ice. In the morning her neighbour, who kept his trees dry, has lost his entire crop, while her trees are fine. Why?
solution: She was protecting the blossoms from a hard frost. As water freezes it gives off heat, and as long as the sprinklers keep adding water, the ice coating stays at exactly zero degrees, which fruit blossom can survive. The air that night fell far below zero, so the neighbour's unprotected blossoms froze solid and died, while hers sat safely inside their ice at zero.
keyFacts: The spraying was deliberate frost protection, not an accident
Freezing water releases heat, so the ice coating holds the blossom at about zero degrees
The open air was much colder than zero, which killed the unprotected blossoms
hints: She did it on purpose, and it worked exactly as she intended.
Ask what temperature the air was that night, and what temperature the ice was.
Water gives off heat as it freezes: a blossom inside constantly refreshed ice stays at zero degrees, while the air around it dropped far lower.

title: A Letter to Herself
situation: A woman spends months filling a notebook. She then photocopies every page, seals the copies in an envelope, addresses it to her own home and posts it. When it arrives a few days later, she does not open it but locks it in a safe, where it stays unopened for years. Why?
solution: She is a songwriter (or novelist) and wants proof of when she created her work in case anyone ever claims it as their own. The post office stamps the sealed envelope with a dated postmark, so an unopened envelope is evidence that the contents existed by that date. If she opened it, the proof would be worthless, so it stays sealed unless she ever needs to produce it in a dispute.
keyFacts: The notebook contains her own creative work (songs, a novel, an invention)
The postmark on the sealed envelope proves the work existed by that date
It must stay sealed so it can serve as evidence if someone steals her work
hints: What is in the envelope matters less than what is printed on the outside of it.
She is protecting something she made against people who might claim it as theirs.
The dated postmark on a still-sealed envelope proves when the pages were written.

title: The Silent Valley
situation: One morning, in the villages beside a deep lake, every person and every animal is found dead. The houses are untouched, there is no sign of violence or disease, and food is still on the tables. Families living higher up the hillsides woke up perfectly healthy and heard nothing in the night. What happened?
solution: The lake sits over volcanic ground, and enormous amounts of carbon dioxide had been dissolving into its deep water for years. One night the gas suddenly burst out of the lake in a huge invisible cloud. Carbon dioxide is heavier than air, so it flowed down into the low-lying villages and pushed the breathable air away, suffocating everyone and everything as they slept. By morning the gas had dispersed, leaving the higher homes untouched.
keyFacts: The victims suffocated because of a gas, not violence, poison or disease
The gas came from the lake (carbon dioxide that had built up in its deep water)
The gas is heavier than air, so it settled in the low areas and spared the hillsides
hints: Nobody and nothing did this on purpose. The lake is the key.
The victims stopped breathing, and the height of your house decided whether you lived.
Something heavier than air came out of the lake in the night and pooled in the valley like water.

title: The Mirrors Nobody Looks At
situation: A small mountain town spent a fortune bolting three enormous mirrors to the cliff high above the rooftops. They are aimed down at the market square, yet nobody ever climbs up to look at them and nobody ever sees their reflection in them. The mayor calls it the best money the town has ever spent, and the café on the square now takes three times as much in January as it used to. Why?
solution: The town sits at the bottom of a steep, narrow valley, so for several months each winter the sun never rises above the surrounding peaks and the square lies in permanent shadow. The mirrors are mounted on motors that track the sun and bounce a bright patch of direct sunlight down onto the square. In midwinter the townspeople now come out to stand and sit in that artificial patch of daylight, which is why the café beside it does so well.
keyFacts: The valley is so deep that direct sunlight never reaches the town for months in winter
The mirrors reflect sunlight from the peaks down into the square
They are motorised and follow the sun so the bright patch stays put
People gather in the sunlit spot, which is why the café's winter takings rose
hints: The mirrors are not there to show anyone an image; they are there to move something.
The town's problem is worst in winter and has nothing to do with snow or wind.
Think about what a deep, narrow valley does to the low winter sun, and what a mirror on a high cliff could do about it.

title: The Ward Nobody Entered
situation: During an occupation, armed soldiers searched a city hospital room by room, hunting for people in hiding. At one corridor the chief physician stopped them, pointed to the letter chalked on the door and quietly explained what the patients inside were suffering from. The soldiers listened to the noises coming from the ward, turned around, and left the building. Every person behind that door survived the war, and not one of them was ill. What was going on?
solution: The people in that ward were refugees the doctors were hiding, and the illness on the door was invented by the doctors themselves: a fictitious, hideously disfiguring and supposedly very contagious disease, complete with fake charts and a fake name. The 'patients' had been coached to cough violently and horribly whenever boots were heard in the corridor. The soldiers were far more frightened of catching the disease than of missing a few fugitives, so they never opened the door, and the fiction kept the hidden people alive until the city was liberated.
keyFacts: The 'patients' were fugitives being hidden by the hospital staff
The disease named on the door did not exist; the doctors invented it
The hidden people faked terrifying symptoms, especially coughing, on cue
The soldiers' fear of contagion made them refuse to search the ward
hints: The doctors were not lying about the patients being in the ward, only about why they were there.
The most powerful weapon in the hospital that day was a name written on a door.
No such illness has ever appeared in any medical textbook, because three doctors made it up that week to keep the soldiers out.

title: The Voice on the Platform
situation: For years, an elderly woman travelled to an underground station she had no reason to use, sat on the platform, let train after train go by, and then went home. One winter she stopped coming, and the staff assumed she had moved away. In fact she was waiting for an answer to a letter she had written to the transport company, and once she got it she came back every week again. Why?
solution: Decades earlier her husband, who had since died, had recorded the safety announcement played on that platform, so sitting there was the only place left where she could still hear his voice. During a system upgrade his recording was replaced by a new digital one, and she stopped visiting because there was nothing to come for. Her letter asked the company whether the old recording still existed anywhere; they tracked it down and put his voice back on that one platform for her.
keyFacts: She went there to listen, not to travel
The recorded station announcement was her late husband's voice
The recording was replaced during a technical upgrade, so she stopped coming
The transport company found the old recording and restored it on that platform
hints: She never intended to board a train, and she was not meeting anybody.
What she came for was a sound, and it belonged to someone who had died.
Her husband's job long ago was to speak the words every passenger on that platform hears.

title: The Passenger Who Never Eats
situation: A woman buys two seats on every long flight she takes, always side by side. Her fellow passenger never queues at the desk, never eats the meal, never speaks to the crew, and is always strapped in by the window before anyone else boards. The crew know exactly who it is and think nothing of it. Who is travelling with her?
solution: She is a professional cellist, and the second seat is for her cello. The instrument is far too valuable and fragile to go into the hold, and too large to fit in an overhead locker, so airlines sell musicians a full seat for it and it is buckled in like any other passenger. It boards early with her, sits by the window out of the aisle, and of course eats nothing.
keyFacts: The second passenger is not a person but an object
It is a large, fragile, valuable musical instrument (a cello)
She buys it a seat because it cannot safely travel as hold luggage and is too big for the cabin lockers
It is strapped into the seat and boards with her
hints: Nobody is being deceived: the airline knows perfectly well what is in that seat.
The passenger has never been alive, and the woman's job explains why she takes it everywhere.
Think about what a musician would never let a baggage handler throw into a cargo hold.

title: The Runner Who Stopped Winning
situation: In the final metres of a race, the runner in second place suddenly finds the leader standing still in front of him with the finish line still ahead. He could stroll past and win. Instead he slows down, stays behind the man, waves his arms at him, and crosses the line second. The crowd, the press and even his own coach call him a hero rather than a fool. Why?
solution: The leader was a foreign athlete who could not read the local signs and had mistaken a banner across the course for the finish, so he pulled up a few metres too early believing he had already won. The second runner realised at once that the man had beaten him fairly and had only been defeated by a misunderstanding. Rather than steal the win on a technicality, he gestured and shepherded the confused leader over the real line ahead of him. He said afterwards that a victory taken that way would not have been his.
keyFacts: The leader stopped by mistake, thinking he had already crossed the finish line
The mistake came from not understanding the local language or signage on the course
The second runner could easily have won but refused to profit from the error
He gestured to guide the leader over the true finish line and deliberately came second
hints: The leader was not injured, ill or cheating; he genuinely believed the race was over.
Something about the course itself misled him, and it would not have misled a local.
The man behind decided that the fastest runner should win, even if the rules would have handed him the trophy.

title: The Village That Was Never There
situation: A mapmaker invents a village out of thin air and prints it at a lonely crossroads on his road map, in a spot where there is nothing but trees. Fourteen years later he finds the same village, with the same invented name, printed on a rival company's map, and he threatens to sue them for copying his work. The rival's lawyers reply with a single photograph, and he quietly drops the case. What was in the photograph?
solution: The invented village was a copyright trap: a fake entry that only a plagiarist could ever reproduce, so its appearance elsewhere would prove theft. But in the years between, someone had driven out to that crossroads with a map, seen the name, and built a shop there, painting the invented name over the door as the name of the place. The photograph showed that building and its sign. Since a real, inhabited place now stood at those coordinates, the rival could say it had mapped reality rather than copied a fiction, and the lawsuit collapsed.
keyFacts: The village was a deliberate fake planted to catch map plagiarists (a copyright trap)
In the meantime a real building, such as a shop, was put up at that crossroads
Its owners took the name from the map, so the invented name became the genuine name of a real place
The photograph proved the place now existed, so the rival was mapping fact, not copying an invention
hints: The mapmaker did not invent the village by accident; the lie had a purpose.
The photograph was taken at that very crossroads, and it showed something that had not been there when he drew the map.
By the time of the argument, the village was no longer imaginary, and you cannot own the name of a real place.

title: The Torn Suit
situation: A man is doing his job when his suit tears. Fifteen minutes later, he is dead. What happened?
solution: The man is an astronaut out on a spacewalk. His spacesuit tears, and he dies from being exposed to the vacuum of space.
keyFacts: He is an astronaut on a spacewalk
The torn suit is his spacesuit, which exposes him to space
hints: He was not at an ordinary workplace.
His suit was the only thing keeping him alive where he worked.
He was working outside, far above the Earth.

title: The Bricks and the Beetle
situation: A dead man lies near a pile of bricks. Nearby, a beetle sits on top of a book. How did he die?
solution: The man was an amateur mechanic working under his car, a Volkswagen Beetle, which he had propped up on a pile of bricks. The car fell off the bricks and crushed him. The book is the Volkswagen service manual, and the 'beetle' on top of it is the car itself.
keyFacts: The beetle is a Volkswagen Beetle car, not an insect
He was a mechanic working under the car
The car was propped on the bricks and fell on him
The book is the car's service manual
hints: The beetle is much bigger than you think.
The man was doing some repairs himself, following instructions from the book.
The beetle has four wheels and was resting on the bricks.

title: The Ship That Stays
situation: At the bottom of a sea lies a ship worth millions of dollars. It will never be recovered. Where is it, and why will nobody bring it back?
solution: The 'ship' is the Eagle, the Apollo 11 lunar module. It landed in the Sea of Tranquility on the Moon, which has no water, and it will probably stay there for the foreseeable future.
keyFacts: The ship is a spacecraft, the Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle
The 'sea' is the Sea of Tranquility on the Moon
hints: This sea contains no water at all.
The ship never sailed. It flew.
Think about 1969 and 'The Eagle has landed.'

title: The Card Game
situation: Two people are playing cards. One of them looks around and suddenly realizes he is going to die. What did he see?
solution: It is dark outside, so the window works like a mirror. The player sees his own reflection in the window but not his companion's. He realizes the other player is a vampire and that he is in mortal danger.
keyFacts: He sees reflections in a dark window
His companion has no reflection
The companion is a vampire
hints: What he saw was not in the cards or on the table.
It was dark outside, and that made the window important.
Something that should have been there in the glass was missing.

title: The Black Town
situation: A black man dressed all in black and wearing a black mask stands at a crossroads in a town painted entirely black. All the streetlights are broken and there is no moon. A black-painted car with no headlights drives straight at him but turns in time and doesn't hit him. How did the driver see him?
solution: It's daytime and the sun is out. The driver could see the man perfectly well, so the missing moon, the broken streetlights and the unlit headlights make no difference.
keyFacts: It is daytime
The sun provides the light, so the driver can see him
hints: Nobody said anything about what time it was.
The streetlights, moon and headlights don't matter at all.
Which light source hasn't been mentioned?

title: A View to Murder
situation: A husband and wife stop at a lookout on a steep mountain range in a remote place to admire the view, with their car parked behind and above them. With nobody near it, the car rolls down the hill and kills the wife. Nobody touches the scene before the police arrive, and an officer inspects the car and immediately arrests the husband for murder. What did the officer see?
solution: The handbrake had not been put on, and there was a large puddle of water under the brake pedal. The officer worked out that the husband had wedged a block of ice against the brake pedal to hold it down. Once the couple were out of the car and standing below it, the ice melted, the brake let go and the car rolled onto the wife.
keyFacts: A block of ice held the brake pedal down
The ice melted and released the car
The officer saw a puddle of water under the brake pedal and the handbrake not set
hints: Nobody moved the car, but something inside it changed while the couple were at the view.
Look closely at the driver's footwell. Something was there that wasn't there before.
Something held the brake down for a while and then quietly disappeared, leaving only water.

title: The Microwave Timer
situation: A man comes home and his wife calls to him from behind the closed bathroom door: 'Welcome home, darling. Dinner's in the microwave. Please look at the timer and tell me how long until it's ready.' He answers her, and then immediately calls the police. Why?
solution: The husband is blind. His wife knows he cannot possibly read a microwave timer, and she would not normally shut the bathroom door on him, so the strange request was a coded message that something was badly wrong. He realised she was in danger and called the police.
keyFacts: The husband is blind
The wife knows he can't read the timer, so the request was a coded distress signal
He realises she is in danger, so he calls the police
hints: The request itself was not really about dinner.
Think about what makes the request impossible for this particular man.
The husband cannot see, and his wife knows that perfectly well.

title: The Answered Prayer
situation: On a wild, stormy night, a woman is running late to deliver some important documents. She races into a lift and presses her floor, but as the lift starts to rise the power goes out and she is stuck. Instead of panicking, she feels her prayers have been answered. Why?
solution: She was carrying a stay of execution for a prisoner due to die in the electric chair only moments later. The power cut that trapped her in the lift also knocked out the electric chair, so the execution could not go ahead. That gave her time to deliver the reprieve. (The site also accepts another answer: the papers were notes her boss needed for a meeting, and the power cut called off the meeting.)
keyFacts: She was delivering a stay of execution
The execution was by electric chair
The power cut stopped the execution and gave her time to deliver the papers
hints: The power cut affected more than just her lift.
Her documents were a matter of life and death for someone else.
Think about a way of carrying out a death sentence that needs electricity.

title: The Angry Cat
situation: Rachael and Thomas move into a new share house. As soon as they arrive, an angry, aggressive cat confronts them, and Thomas is very upset about it. Rachael knows there isn't really a problem, and that even if she does nothing at all, Thomas will soon be fine with the new place. Why?
solution: Thomas is a cat himself. The 'angry cat' is his own reflection in a mirror in the new house, which he takes for a rival cat challenging him. Rachael knows he will get used to it, so there is nothing she needs to do.
keyFacts: Thomas is a cat
The angry cat is Thomas's reflection in a mirror
hints: Don't assume Thomas and Rachael are both people.
The angry cat copies Thomas's every move.
Something in the new house shows Thomas his own face.

title: Close Call
situation: A man receives a phone call, and before he can even answer it, the call has saved the life of the man standing next to him. How?
solution: The site's first answer is that the two men were in a war zone, and an enemy sniper had the second man in his crosshairs. When the phone rang, its light drew the sniper's eye to the first man, so he switched targets and the man next to him was spared. The site also lists other answers: the man was an executioner who stopped when he saw the Governor calling, or the ringing phone warned the second man of an approaching attacker so he could get away.
keyFacts: A sniper was aiming at the second man
The phone's light drew the sniper's attention
The sniper switched targets to the man with the phone, sparing his companion
hints: Someone who wanted to kill the second man was watching from far away.
It isn't what the caller said. The call was never answered. It's what the phone did when it rang.
In the dark, a lit-up phone screen is easy to spot through a rifle scope.

title: The Bus Stop
situation: On a stormy night, a man driving along a rural road passes a bus stop where three people are waiting. One is an elderly woman who needs medical attention, one is his best friend who once saved his life, and one is an attractive woman he would love to meet. His car has room for only one passenger. What does he do?
solution: He stops at the bus stop and gets out of the car himself. He hands his car to his best friend, who is great at helping people, and asks him to drive the old lady to the hospital. The man then stays behind and waits for the bus with the young woman, keeping her safe until it comes.
keyFacts: He gives his car to his best friend
The friend drives the elderly woman to hospital
He waits for the bus with the woman he wants to meet
hints: You're assuming the man has to be the one driving.
The car can still carry one passenger even if the driver changes.
What if he got out and let someone else take the wheel?

title: The Cheating Husband
situation: A newly married woman comes home from work early and finds her husband in bed with another woman. Almost at once, her anger fades. Why?
solution: Her new and devoted husband had been using her hours at work to delete videos and images of his past romantic encounters. The 'other woman' she saw him in bed with was only in one of those old recordings, not really there. Once she understood he was getting rid of his past for her sake, she was no longer angry.
keyFacts: The other woman was not physically there
She was in old videos or images from his past
He was deleting them out of devotion to his wife
hints: Nobody else was really in the room.
Think about screens and recordings.
He was busy erasing his romantic past before his wife got home.

title: The Movie Theater
situation: A man takes a woman to see a film. Halfway through, he kills her with a knife, a murder he had planned in advance. Afterwards they leave the theater together, and nobody notices a thing. How?
solution: The couple were at a drive-in theater, watching the film from inside their car. The car had tinted windows, so nobody could see in. When the film ended, he simply drove out with her body still in the car, so they 'left together'.
keyFacts: It was a drive-in theater
They were inside a car with tinted windows
He drove away with her body in the car
hints: Not every theater has rows of seats.
The whole thing happened out of everyone's sight.
They never left their car at all.

title: The Oyster Diver
situation: A man who dives for oysters comes face to face with a dangerous shark. Yet he isn't the least bit worried. Why not?
solution: The shark was a loan shark, and the diver owed him money. That day he got lucky and found a valuable pearl inside one of his oysters. The pearl easily covered the debt, so he had nothing to fear.
keyFacts: The shark is a loan shark, not a fish
The diver owed him money
He found a valuable pearl that paid off the debt
hints: The shark wasn't in the water.
Some sharks deal in money.
His catch that day made him rich enough to pay back what he owed.

title: The Long Search
situation: Betty went missing more than 50 years ago. One day someone finds her, though they weren't looking for her at all. They know straight away that it is Betty. How?
solution: Betty was a boat that had mysteriously disappeared. A diver came across the wreck by chance. The name 'Betty' was still written on the bow.
keyFacts: Betty is a boat
A diver found the wreck
Her name was still on the bow
hints: Betty isn't a person.
She was found underwater.
Her name was painted on her.

title: Explain This Death
situation: A man reads a newspaper story about Mr and Mrs Smith, who were on a skiing holiday in the Alps. Mrs Smith fell and was killed. The reader immediately knows Mr Smith murdered her. How?
solution: The man reading the paper was the travel agent who had sold Mr Smith the tickets for the trip. Mr Smith had bought a return ticket for himself but only a one-way ticket for his wife. He clearly never expected her to come home.
keyFacts: The reader is the travel agent who booked the trip
Mr Smith bought a return ticket for himself
He bought only a one-way ticket for his wife
hints: The reader knows something about the trip from before it happened.
Think about who arranged the holiday.
Compare the tickets the couple were each booked on.

title: The Curious Guilt Puzzle
situation: Jenny is found dead in her car after a violent attack, and her purse and phone are missing. The police contact her husband and ask him to come in. As soon as he arrives, they arrest him. Why?
solution: The police had never told him where the crime scene was. The husband went straight to the right location anyway. Only the killer could have known where Jenny's body was.
keyFacts: The police did not tell him where she was
He arrived at the crime scene anyway
Knowing the location gave him away as the killer
hints: What matters is where he turned up.
Think about what the police did and didn't tell him on the phone.
How did he know where to go?

title: The Pitchfork
situation: Jason is working in his garden with a pitchfork while witnesses look on. A masked gunman fires a single shot at him, and Jason charges at him in a zigzag and kills him with the pitchfork. The witnesses call him brave and point out a bullet hole through his jacket, but Jason was never in danger and was no hero. Why?
solution: The masked man owed Jason money. Jason told him he had to die in a way that would let his family claim insurance and pay off the debt. Jason supplied the gun himself: a homemade pistol that could hold only one round, which he loaded with a blank before permanently sealing the chamber so it could fire only once. The 'attack' was staged so Jason could kill the man in apparent self-defense.
keyFacts: The gunman owed Jason a debt
His death was arranged so his family could claim insurance
Jason supplied the gun, loaded with a blank
The one-shot homemade gun's chamber was sealed, so it could not be reloaded
hints: Jason and the gunman knew each other.
The weapon came from Jason, and it could only ever fire once.
The shot was a blank, and the man's death was meant to pay off money he owed Jason through insurance.

title: The Astronaut's Despair
situation: A lone spaceship pilot crash-lands on an unknown, uninhabited planet whose air will keep him alive for only an hour. Nobody knows where he is, and his wrecked ship has no breathable air left. He sets off to explore with no equipment, and thirty minutes later a human voice startles him. How?
solution: In his despair, the astronaut cried out in anguish. What he heard was his own echo coming back to him. There was nobody else on the planet.
keyFacts: There is nobody else on the planet
He cried out in despair
The voice was his own echo
hints: The voice didn't belong to anyone new.
Think about what he did when he realised how hopeless things were.
Sound can bounce back off the landscape.

title: Which Light Switch?
situation: Upstairs there are three switches, and only one of them works the light in a cellar at the bottom of some rickety stairs. The cellar is so hard to reach that you can go down only once, and from upstairs you cannot tell whether the light is on. How can you work out which switch controls the light?
solution: Turn the first switch on and leave it for several minutes, then turn it off and turn on the second switch. Go down to the cellar. If the bulb is lit, it is the second switch; if it is off but warm, it is the first; if it is off and cold, it is the third.
keyFacts: Leave one switch on long enough to heat the bulb, then turn it off
Turn a second switch on before going down
Lit bulb = second switch, warm bulb = first switch, cold bulb = third switch
hints: A light bulb tells you more than whether it is on or off.
Think about what happens to a bulb that has been on for a while.
Touch the bulb: heat shows which switch was on earlier.

title: Til Death Do Us Part
situation: A wife plans to kill her husband in a way that makes a successful prosecution against her unlikely. She breaks something in their home so that she has a reason to send her husband somewhere. The husband has no idea what she intends, and he dies. What did she break, and how did it lead to his death?
solution: The husband was on life support at home. His wife broke the life-support equipment, which meant he had to be rushed to a hospital. She had him taken to a hospital across the state border, where euthanasia is legal, unlike in their home state. There his life was ended legally, so she was unlikely ever to be convicted.
keyFacts: The husband was on life support at home
She broke the life-support equipment, so he had to be moved to hospital
The hospital was across a state border where euthanasia is legal
His death was legal there, so prosecuting her would be hard
hints: The husband could not look after himself and depended on something in the house.
What she broke was a machine that kept him alive, so he had to be moved at once.
Where he was taken mattered: across the border, the law on ending a life is different.

title: Survival
situation: A baby falls out of a window of a 20-story building, yet survives. How?
solution: It was a ground-floor window. The building has 20 stories, but the baby fell from a window on the lowest floor, so the drop was tiny. (The page also gives an alternative answer: the baby and its mother, who jumped out after it, were birds.)
keyFacts: The baby fell from a ground-floor window
The height of the building has nothing to do with the fall
hints: Don't assume the height of the building tells you how far the baby fell.
A 20-story building has windows on every floor, not just the top ones.
Which floor was the window on?

title: The Deadly Door
situation: A man dies as a result of walking through a door. The door itself doesn't harm him. How did he die?
solution: He opened the external door of an aircraft mid-flight and went through it, falling to his death. The page accepts other answers too: he opened the door of a lion's cage, or he opened the jail cell of a homicidal maniac after being told not to. Its clue says he might just be an idiot.
keyFacts: The danger was on the other side of the door, not the door itself
He opened an aircraft's outer door mid-flight and fell out (or another door onto deadly danger, such as a lion's cage)
hints: The door was perfectly ordinary; the danger was on the other side of it.
He was not on the ground when he opened it.
He was on an aeroplane in flight, and he opened the outside door.

title: Frozen in Midsummer
situation: In the middle of summer, a body is found in a park in Chicago. It has a fractured skull and many other broken bones. Yet the cause of death was hypothermia. How can this be?
solution: The man was a stowaway who had hidden in the landing gear compartment of an airplane. High up during the flight, he froze to death. When the plane lowered its landing gear to land, his body fell out and landed in the park, which broke his skull and his other bones.
keyFacts: He was a stowaway in an airplane's landing gear compartment
He froze to death at high altitude during the flight
His body fell out when the landing gear opened, causing the broken bones
hints: The cold that killed him was not in Chicago.
He was very high up for several hours before he ended up in the park.
He was hiding somewhere on an airplane that is not heated, and it opens just before landing.

title: The Smoking Car
situation: A man is travelling home from Switzerland by train. If he had been sitting in a non-smoking car, he would have died. Why?
solution: The man had been blind and had gone to Switzerland for an operation that gave him back his sight. On the way home the train went into a tunnel and everything went dark. He thought he had gone blind again and was ready to kill himself, until he saw the glowing cigarettes of the other passengers and knew he could still see.
keyFacts: He had just had surgery that restored his sight
The train went through a dark tunnel and he thought he was blind again
The glow of the other passengers' cigarettes showed him he could still see, so he didn't kill himself
hints: The smoke itself has nothing to do with it. Something about the cigarettes mattered to his eyes.
Why he went to Switzerland matters: he was there for medical treatment.
When the train went into a tunnel, only the lit cigarettes told him he wasn't blind again.

title: Five Minutes of Radio
situation: A man is driving his car. He turns on the radio and listens for five minutes. Then he turns around, drives home, and shoots his wife. Why?
solution: He was listening to a radio contest show that phones a number live on air. The number the show announced and called was the phone in his own bedroom. A man's voice answered, so he knew his wife was with another man, and he went home and shot her.
keyFacts: A radio contest program called a phone number live on air
It was his own bedroom phone number
A man answered, revealing his wife was being unfaithful
hints: It matters what kind of programme was on the radio.
He heard something on air that connected directly to his own home.
The show phoned his bedroom, and the person who answered was not his wife.

title: The Rope and the Bell
situation: A rope breaks. A bell rings. A man dies. What happened?
solution: A blind man used to walk near a cliff, judging how far he was from the edge by the sound of a bell buoy out in the water. The rope anchoring the buoy broke and it drifted further from shore. Going by the sound of the bell, he misjudged the distance and walked over the edge of the cliff.
keyFacts: The man was blind and used the sound of a bell buoy to judge where the cliff edge was
The buoy's anchor rope broke and it drifted away
He misjudged the distance and walked off the cliff
hints: The bell was not in a church, and it was not meant for him.
The man couldn't see, so he found his way by sound.
The bell was on a buoy he used to tell where the cliff edge was. Once its rope broke, the buoy drifted out of place.

title: The New Shoes
situation: A woman buys a new pair of shoes and goes to work. That day, she dies. How did the shoes kill her?
solution: She was a knife-thrower's assistant in a circus. Her new shoes had higher heels than the ones she usually wore, which made her taller. The knife-thrower aimed as he always did, misjudged because of her new height, and a knife struck and killed her.
keyFacts: She was a circus knife-thrower's assistant
Her new shoes had higher heels, which changed her height
The thrower's aim was off and a knife hit her
hints: Her job put her in danger every day, but it was always carefully measured.
She stood still at work while someone else aimed at her.
The heels made her a little taller, and the knives were thrown with a set height in mind.

title: The Returning Tourists
situation: During World War II, two German spies, Hans and Fritz, try to get into America by posing as American tourists returning home. Fritz gets through. Hans is arrested on the spot. What gave him away?
solution: On arrival, both men had to fill in forms that asked for their birthdays. Fritz wrote 7/7/15, which reads the same in any format. Hans wrote 20/6/18 instead of 6/20/18, putting the day before the month the European way, which showed he was not an American.
keyFacts: They had to fill in forms with their dates of birth
Hans wrote his date in European day/month order
Americans write month/day, so this showed he wasn't American; Fritz's date (7/7/15) looked the same either way
hints: He gave himself away with paperwork, not by anything he said.
The form asked for a simple personal detail: his date of birth.
Americans and Europeans write dates in different orders. Fritz's birthday looks the same both ways.

title: The Locked Room Fire
situation: In France in 1959, a woman waits in her room for her husband to come home, with all the doors locked from the inside. When he arrives, the house has burned to the ground and she is dead. How did the fire start?
solution: Sunlight bounced off her large mirror and was focused onto her lingerie, heating it until it caught fire. She was so absorbed in reading that she didn't notice the warmth until her clothing was alight. Because the doors were locked from the inside, nobody could get in to reach her.
keyFacts: Sunlight reflected by her mirror was focused onto her clothing
The heat set her lingerie on fire
She was absorbed in reading and didn't notice; the locked doors kept rescuers out
hints: Nobody else started the fire, and it wasn't an accident with a flame.
Something ordinary in her room concentrated heat from outside.
The sun reflected off a mirror onto what she was wearing while she sat reading.

title: The Cloudy-Day Corner
situation: On my way to work by motorcycle, there is one corner that I take at a certain speed whether it's rainy or sunny. But if it's cloudy and not raining, I usually go faster. Why?
solution: There is a car wash by that corner. On rainy days the road is wet from the rain, and on sunny days it is wet from all the cars being washed, so traction is poor either way. On cloudy days people expect rain and don't bother washing their cars, so the road stays dry and he can take the corner faster.
keyFacts: There is a car wash near the corner
The road is wet on rainy days from rain and on sunny days from car-wash water
On cloudy days few people wash their cars, so the road is dry
hints: What matters is how slippery the road is.
On sunny days, water still ends up on that corner from somewhere.
There's a car wash nearby. Who washes their car when it looks like it's about to rain?

title: Thirty Countries Without a Passport
situation: An ordinary American citizen with no passport visits more than thirty foreign countries in one day. He is welcomed in every one of them and leaves each of his own accord. How?
solution: He is a mail courier who delivers packages to foreign embassies in the United States. The grounds of an embassy legally belong to the country it represents, so each delivery counts as a visit to a foreign country.
keyFacts: He delivers mail or packages to foreign embassies
The embassies are in the United States
Embassy grounds count as the territory of their country
hints: He never leaves his own country.
His job takes him to many official buildings in one city.
He delivers to embassies, and each embassy counts as foreign soil.

title: The Birthday Cologne
situation: For his birthday, a man's wife gives him a new cologne, and he tries it on. He then goes out to get some food and is killed. What happened?
solution: The man was a beekeeper, and he went out to collect food from his hives. The new cologne changed his smell, so the bees didn't recognise him. They attacked him in huge numbers and killed him. The source notes that this was reportedly based on a real attack.
keyFacts: He was a beekeeper
The food he went out for came from his hives (honey)
The cologne changed his smell, so the bees didn't recognise him and attacked
hints: He didn't go to a shop or a restaurant to get the food.
The animals he worked with knew him by his smell.
He kept bees, and the new scent made them treat him as an intruder.

title: The Unpunishable Sister
situation: In court, a woman has undeniable proof that her sister murdered her husband. The judge says it is the strangest case he has ever seen: the case is cut and dried, yet the guilty woman cannot be punished. Why not?
solution: The two sisters are Siamese twins, joined together. Any punishment given to the murderer, such as prison, would also fall on her innocent sister. So even though her guilt is proven, she cannot be punished.
keyFacts: The sisters are Siamese (conjoined) twins
Punishing the guilty sister would also punish the innocent one
hints: The trouble is not with the evidence or the law.
Think about what would happen to the woman who brought the case if her sister were jailed.
The two sisters can never be apart.

title: The Sawdust in the Corner
situation: A man lies dead in a room. In one corner is a small pile of pieces of wood and some sawdust. What happened?
solution: The dead man was a blind midget who worked in a circus, and he checked his height every day against his walking cane. A jealous fellow midget sawed a little off the cane each night. Measuring against the shrinking cane, the blind man thought he was growing too tall to keep his job as a midget. In despair at losing his livelihood, he killed himself.
keyFacts: The dead man was a blind circus midget
Someone jealous sawed a bit off his cane every night
He used the cane to check his height and thought he was growing
Fearing he would lose his job, he killed himself
hints: The wood came from something the man used every day.
His job depended on staying a certain size, and he could not see.
Someone was secretly cutting his walking cane shorter, and he measured himself against it.

title: The Fatal Flash
situation: There is a flash of light, and a man dies. What happened?
solution: The man was a lion-tamer posing for photographs with his lions. The flash from the camera startled the lions. They attacked him and mauled him to death.
keyFacts: The man was a lion-tamer
The flash came from a camera
The flash frightened the lions, which mauled him
hints: The light itself did not hurt him.
He was posing for a picture at work, and he was not alone.
The animals he worked with did not like the camera flash.

title: The Silent Phone Call
situation: A man is sitting in bed. He makes a phone call, says nothing, and then goes to sleep. Why?
solution: The man was staying in a hotel and could not sleep because the guest in the next room was snoring. He phoned that room, and the ringing woke the snorer up. Before his neighbour could fall asleep and start snoring again, the man got to sleep himself.
keyFacts: He was in a hotel and the person next door was snoring
The call was only meant to wake the snorer
He fell asleep before the snoring started again
hints: He wasn't trying to talk to anyone. The call itself did the job.
He was not at home, and the walls were thin.
A noise from the next room was keeping him awake.

title: The Surprise Inside
situation: A man kills his wife outside their house. He then goes inside the house and kills himself. Why?
solution: The man had embezzled money and planned to kill his wife and start a new life with it. He killed her on the front step of their home, then went inside. There, friends who had gathered for a surprise birthday party switched on the lights and shouted 'Surprise!' With so many witnesses to his crime, he took his own life.
keyFacts: He planned to murder his wife and escape with embezzled money
Friends were hiding inside for a surprise party
They saw him right after the murder, so he killed himself
hints: He had planned the murder and did not plan to kill himself.
Something unexpected was waiting inside the house.
It was a special day, and the house was full of people hiding in the dark.

title: The Stopped Elevator
situation: A man gets into an elevator. When the elevator stops, he knows his wife is dead. How?
solution: The man was leaving a hospital after visiting his wife, who was being kept alive on life-support machines. The elevator stopped because the power had failed. He realised this meant the emergency backup generator had failed too, so her life-support machines had stopped and she could not survive.
keyFacts: His wife was on life support in a hospital
The elevator stopped because of a power failure
That meant the backup power had failed and her machines had stopped
hints: The elevator didn't stop at a floor. It stopped between floors.
His wife depended on a machine to stay alive.
They were in a hospital, and the elevator lost power.

title: The Flickering Lights
situation: A man runs along a corridor with a piece of paper in his hand. The lights flicker, and the man drops to his knees and cries out, 'Oh no!' What happened?
solution: The paper was a pardon for a prisoner who had been condemned to die. The man was rushing to deliver it before the execution. When the lights flickered, he knew the electric chair had just been used and the prisoner was already dead.
keyFacts: The paper was a pardon for a condemned prisoner
The execution was by electric chair
The flickering lights showed the execution had just happened, so he was too late
hints: The piece of paper could have saved someone's life.
He is in a prison.
The lights dimmed because a lot of power was suddenly being used.

title: In the Dark
situation: If he had turned on the light, he would have lived. What happened?
solution: A shopkeeper was shot during a robbery. Bleeding and dazed, he made his way to the telephone in the back room and tried to call for help without turning on the light, dialling by feel. He was used to his cash register keypad, but a telephone's number buttons are arranged the other way up. He reached a stranger who could not find him, so help never came.
keyFacts: He was a shopkeeper shot in a robbery
He dialled for help in the dark, by feel
He mixed up the phone keypad with the upside-down cash register keypad
He reached the wrong person, so help never arrived
hints: He was already badly hurt and was trying to get help.
He could not see the telephone buttons.
He worked with another keypad every day, and its numbers are laid out differently from a phone's.

title: The Burning Cigarette
situation: A man in uniform stands on the beach of a tropical island. He lights a cigarette and starts reading a letter. The cigarette burns down between his fingers, but he doesn't throw it away. He cries. Why?
solution: The man was a guard at a leper colony. The letter confirmed that he had caught leprosy. Leprosy destroys the nerves that sense pain but leaves the ability to move, so he could hold the cigarette but could not feel it burning him. That showed him the diagnosis was true.
keyFacts: He was a guard at a leper colony
The letter said he had leprosy
Leprosy kills feeling but not movement, so he could not feel the cigarette burning
hints: He doesn't throw the cigarette away because he can't feel it.
His job on the island put him close to sick people.
The letter gave him a medical diagnosis, and the disease destroys feeling.

title: The Motel Horn
situation: A man leaves his motel room, goes out to his car, and honks the horn. Why?
solution: It was the middle of the night, and after going to his car the man could not remember which room was his. He honked the horn, and the noise woke the other guests, who switched on their lights. His wife was deaf and did not hear it, so the one room that stayed dark was his.
keyFacts: It was night and he could not find his own room
His wife was deaf
The horn woke everyone else, so his was the only room that stayed dark
hints: He wasn't trying to call anyone to the car.
He had forgotten something about where he was staying.
The person in his room couldn't hear the horn, but the other guests could.

title: The Yacht and the Corpses
situation: A yacht sits in the middle of the ocean. Several corpses are floating in the water near it. Nobody attacked them and the yacht is undamaged. What happened?
solution: The people on the yacht decided to go for a swim one afternoon and dived into the sea. They forgot to put the ladder down first, so once they were in the water they had no way to climb back up the yacht's sides, and they all drowned. In a variant, they did put a ladder down, but it only just reached the water. When they dived in, the lightened boat rose higher and left the ladder out of reach.
keyFacts: The dead people were the yacht's own passengers who went swimming
They could not climb back aboard because there was no ladder, or it was out of reach
They drowned beside their own boat
hints: Nobody else was involved: the dead were the people from the yacht.
They went into the water on purpose, for fun.
Getting into the water was easy. Getting back out onto the boat was the problem.

title: The Man from the Sea
situation: Abel walks out of the ocean. Cain asks him who he is, and Abel answers. Cain then kills Abel. Why?
solution: Abel was the prince of an island nation. He survived a shipwreck that killed his father, the king, and was stranded on a deserted island, where he built a raft. While he was gone, a regent ruled his homeland and brought it peace and prosperity. When Abel finally came home, a native fisherman named Cain recognized that the prince's return and claim to the throne would threaten that peace, so he killed him with whatever was at hand, such as driftwood.
keyFacts: Abel was a lost prince or heir returning home after a shipwreck
His homeland had become peaceful and prosperous under someone else while he was gone
Cain killed him to stop him reclaiming power and to preserve the peace
hints: Abel's answer to 'Who are you?' was what sealed his fate.
Abel had been missing for a long time, and things at home had changed while he was away, for the better.
Abel was royalty, and his return would have upset a new order that was working well.

title: The Two Cruises
situation: A man takes a two-week cruise from the U.S. to Mexico. Shortly after he returns, he takes a three-day cruise that stops at no other ports. He stays in his cabin both times. He makes $250,000. How?
solution: The man is a smuggler. During the first cruise, the contraband is delivered to his cabin and he hides it in the air-conditioning duct, then passes through customs with nothing on him. For the second, three-day cruise he books the same cabin on the same ship and collects the hidden goods. Because that cruise never stops at a foreign port, he walks off without a customs inspection.
keyFacts: He is a smuggler
He hid the contraband in his cabin (in the air duct) on the first cruise, so customs found nothing
On the second cruise, with no foreign stops, he took the same cabin and brought the goods off without inspection
hints: The money is not legal.
Where he stays on the ship matters: it is the same place both times.
The second trip goes nowhere foreign, so nobody checks what he carries off.

title: The Dinner Invitation
situation: A woman invited them to dinner, and because of it she lost her job. What happened?
solution: Suzy, a buyer for a museum, invited an elderly archaeologist named Harry to a business dinner. Harry often talked about 'Jane', so she assumed Jane was his wife and invited them both. In fact Jane was his famous discovery, an ancient skeleton he had named in the style of 'Lucy'. Harry was offended that she didn't know, complained to her boss, and Suzy was fired.
keyFacts: She invited a man and 'Jane', assuming Jane was his wife
Jane was actually an ancient skeleton he had discovered and named
He was offended and her employer fired her for not knowing
hints: Her work put her in contact with experts in a scholarly field.
One of the 'them' she invited was not a living person.
Think of the famous fossil skeleton named Lucy.

title: The Unpaid Meal
situation: A man goes into a restaurant, eats a big meal, and leaves. He never pays for it, yet he did nothing wrong. How?
solution: The man was a famous artist, and he paid for his meal by check. An autograph collector saw him eating, then bought the signed check from the restaurant manager. Because the check was kept for the signature and never cashed, the meal was never actually paid for.
keyFacts: He was a famous artist and paid with a signed check
A collector bought the check from the restaurant for the signature
The check was never cashed, so no money ever left his account
hints: He did try to pay in the usual way.
The man is famous, and his name is worth something.
The restaurant sold the piece of paper he signed instead of cashing it.

title: Into the Fire
situation: One man ran into a fire and lived. Another man stayed where there was no fire and died. How?
solution: Both men were working in a room protected by a carbon dioxide fire-extinguishing system. When fire broke out next to the room, one man ran out through the flames and escaped with minor burns. The other stayed in the room, the system flooded it with CO2, and he suffocated. A variant has the same thing happen with a halon system.
keyFacts: They were in a room protected by an automatic CO2 (or halon) fire-suppression system
The man who ran through the fire escaped with minor burns
The man who stayed was suffocated by the gas released to put out the fire
hints: Fire was not what killed the man who died.
The room had a special system for fighting fires.
That system works by removing the oxygen from the room.

title: The Interrupted Writer
situation: A writer whose work is seen by millions of people insists that he must never be interrupted while he works. One day he is interrupted, and he never writes again. Why?
solution: The writer was a skywriter, writing messages in the sky with his plane for crowds below. The 'interruption' was another plane colliding with his in mid-air while he was working, and he was killed in the crash.
keyFacts: He was a skywriter who writes with an airplane
He was interrupted by a mid-air collision with another plane
He died, so he never wrote again
hints: He does not write with a pen or a keyboard.
Millions can see his work because it appears somewhere very large and very public.
He writes in the sky, and the interruption came from another aircraft.

title: The Empty Tank
situation: Mr. Browning is very glad that a car ran out of gas. Why?
solution: Soon after their wedding, Mrs. Browning became depressed and the couple had their first fight, and Mr. Browning stormed out. She went into the garage and ran the car, meaning to kill herself with the exhaust fumes. The car soon ran out of gas, so she was still alive when Mr. Browning came back, found her and got help.
keyFacts: His wife tried to kill herself with car exhaust fumes in the garage
The car ran out of gas before the fumes could kill her
He came home in time to find her and get help
hints: The car was not being driven anywhere.
Someone he loves was in danger, and the empty tank saved her.
The car's engine was running inside a closed garage.

title: The Capsized Riverboat
situation: A riverboat full of passengers suddenly turns over, and most of the people on board drown. There was no storm, no collision and no damage to the hull. What happened?
solution: The boat was travelling along a river in India when a large snake dropped onto the deck. The panicked passengers all rushed to the other side of the boat at once, which made it tip over and sink. The source says this is based on a real incident reported in the World Almanac.
keyFacts: A snake fell onto the deck
The passengers all rushed to one side at the same moment
The sudden shift of weight capsized the boat
hints: The passengers themselves caused the boat to turn over.
Something frightening suddenly arrived on board.
A large snake dropped onto the deck and everyone fled to the far side.

title: The Man in the Mask
situation: A man was afraid to go home. The reason was that the man in the mask was there. Where is he, and why is he afraid?
solution: They are playing baseball. The man in the mask is the catcher. The other man is a runner who is afraid to go on to home base because the catcher is waiting there.
keyFacts: It is a baseball game
The man in the mask is the catcher
'Home' means home base, not his house
hints: 'Home' may not mean the place where he lives.
The man in the mask is not a criminal. He wears the mask for protection.
Think of a sport where a player in a mask crouches at home plate.

title: Piece of Paper on the Cactus
situation: A man walks up to a cactus and looks at a piece of paper pinned to it. Then he kills himself. Why?
solution: The man has been wandering lost in the desert and fears he has been walking in circles. To test this, he pinned a blank piece of paper to a cactus and set off walking. When he comes across the same paper again, his fears are confirmed and he knows he will never find his way out.
keyFacts: He is lost in the desert
He pinned the paper there himself as a marker
Finding it again proves he has been walking in circles and cannot escape
hints: Nothing is written on the paper.
The man put the paper there himself earlier.
He is lost in the desert and used the paper to check whether he was going round in circles.

title: Headlights Off
situation: Two men drive toward each other with their headlights off. No moon or stars can be seen, there are no electric lights anywhere nearby, and both cars are painted black with no reflective surfaces. Yet both men know exactly when to hit the brakes, and they narrowly avoid hitting each other. How is this possible?
solution: It is daytime. It is also a cloudy day, which is why the star we call the sun cannot be seen. The drivers simply see each other in the daylight.
keyFacts: It is daytime
The sun is hidden by clouds, so no star is visible
hints: You may be assuming something about the time.
The puzzle never says it is night.
The sun is a star, and clouds are hiding it.

title: This Man Is My Son
situation: A surgeon is called in for an emergency operation. On seeing the patient's face, the surgeon says, 'I cannot operate on this man. This man is my son.' Yet the surgeon is not the patient's father. How is this possible?
solution: The surgeon is the patient's mother.
keyFacts: The surgeon is a woman
The surgeon is the patient's mother
hints: Question what you pictured when you read the word 'surgeon'.
The surgeon really is the patient's parent.
Every son has two parents.

title: The Kiss
situation: A man kisses his daughter. Straight away he regrets it. Why?
solution: The man is King Midas. Everything he touches turns to gold, so when he kisses his daughter she turns into a golden statue.
keyFacts: The man is King Midas
His touch turns things to gold, so his daughter turns to gold
hints: The man is not a real historical person.
He is a king from Greek myth who was granted a wish.
Everything he touches turns into a precious metal.

title: Little Susie
situation: Little Susie's parents told her never to open the basement door. Why?
solution: Susie lived in the basement, and her parents had never let her out. The rule was not there to keep her from going down into the basement. It was there to stop her from leaving it.
keyFacts: Susie lives in the basement
Her parents keep her locked in
The rule stops her getting out, not going in
hints: Think about which side of the door Susie is on.
Nothing dangerous is hidden in the basement.
Susie has never been allowed to leave the basement.

title: Friend on a Plane
situation: A man is sitting on an airplane. He sees his friend come on board and greets him. He is arrested at once. Why?
solution: His friend's name is Jack, and he greeted him by calling out, 'Hi, Jack!' On a plane, that sounds like 'hijack', so he was arrested.
keyFacts: The friend is called Jack
The greeting 'Hi, Jack!' sounds like 'hijack'
hints: The trouble is in exactly what he said.
His friend's name matters.
Say the greeting out loud: a common greeting followed by a short man's name.

title: Photo with Grandfather
situation: A young woman has her photo taken with her grandfather. They have never met before, and neither of them knows they are related. How can this be?
solution: The woman is a medical student. She has her photo taken with a human skeleton that is used for teaching in her classroom. She does not know that the skeleton is her grandfather, who donated his body to science.
keyFacts: She is a medical student
The 'grandfather' is a skeleton used for teaching
He donated his body to science
hints: Her grandfather is not alive.
The photo is taken in a place where people study the human body.
He gave his body to science, and it now stands in her classroom.

title: Draws a Picture, Then Suicide
situation: A woman finishes a drawing. Then she kills herself. Why?
solution: The woman had long been suspicious about her family history, so she did the research needed to draw her family tree. When she finished it, it confirmed that she was the child of incest. She could not live with that fact.
keyFacts: The drawing is her family tree
It reveals she is the product of incest
She had long suspected something about her family history
hints: The drawing is not art. It records information.
Making it took research into her relatives.
It is a family tree, and it shows her parents were closely related to each other.

title: The Stranger
situation: A man finds his wife dead, and there is a stranger in the room with her. What happened?
solution: His wife died in childbirth. The 'stranger' is their newborn baby, whom the man has never seen before.
keyFacts: The wife died giving birth
The stranger is their newborn baby
hints: Nobody committed a crime.
The stranger is very new to the world.
The man has just become a father.

title: The Poker Game Raid
situation: The police burst in on a carpenter, a lorry driver, a mechanic and a fireman who are playing poker together. They have come for a suspect called John. Straight away they know that the fireman is the one they want. How?
solution: The fireman is the only man in the room. The other three poker players, the carpenter, the lorry driver and the mechanic, are all women. Since John is a man's name, the police know at once that he must be the fireman.
keyFacts: The fireman is the only man at the table
The carpenter, lorry driver and mechanic are women
hints: Think about what the police know about John besides his name.
Don't assume anything about the people from their jobs.
What if three of the players could not possibly be called John?

title: The Gas Station Owner
situation: A small-town gas station owner says: 'I'd rather fill two cars from out of town than one car from this town.' Filling one car is less work than filling two. Why does he feel this way?
solution: The people in his town buy their gasoline on credit, so he has to wait to be paid and may never get the money. Visitors from out of town have to pay cash on the spot. Two out-of-town customers put money in his hand, while a local only adds to his list of debts.
keyFacts: Locals buy their gas on credit
Out-of-towners pay cash immediately
hints: The difference is not in the cars or how much gas they take.
Think about when and how he gets paid.
The locals all know him well enough to say 'put it on my tab'.

title: Born in May, Married His Mother
situation: A man says: 'I was born in May, yet my birthday is in June.' He adds that he legally married his own mother. He is telling the truth, and nothing illegal or improper happened. How can this be?
solution: He was physically born in a village called May, and his birthday falls in June. He later became an ordained minister and conducted his mother's wedding ceremony, so he 'married' her to her husband in the legal sense. Both statements play on double meanings.
keyFacts: May is the name of the village where he was born
His birthday is in June
He is a minister who performed his mother's wedding ceremony
hints: Both statements rely on a word with two meanings.
'Born in May' doesn't have to refer to a month.
Think about who says 'I now pronounce you husband and wife'.

title: The Two Barbers
situation: A town has only two barbers. One has a very clean shop and a neat haircut. The other has a messy shop and a scruffy haircut. Which one should you go to for a good haircut, and why?
solution: You should go to the barber with the scruffy haircut. With only two barbers in town, each one must cut the other's hair. The neat barber's good haircut was done by the scruffy barber, so the scruffy one is the better stylist.
keyFacts: Choose the barber with the scruffy haircut
The two barbers cut each other's hair
The neat barber's good haircut is the scruffy barber's work
hints: A barber can't easily cut his own hair.
Who gave each barber his haircut?
There are only two barbers in town, so they must use each other.

title: All Windows Face the Same Way
situation: A man lives in a house where every window in every room, on every side of the house, faces the same direction. It is an ordinary house with windows on all four walls. How is this possible?
solution: He lives at the North Pole. From the North Pole, every direction is south, so every window on every side of the house faces south.
keyFacts: The house is at the North Pole
Every window faces south
hints: The house is ordinary. What matters is where it is.
Think about compass directions at an extreme spot on Earth.
From one particular point, whichever way you look is the same direction.

title: Henry Ford's Soup Test
