situation: When Henry Ford was considering someone for a senior position, he often took the candidate out to lunch and ordered soup for them. He watched closely as the soup arrived. What was he looking for?
solution: He watched whether the candidate added salt to the soup before tasting it. Salting before tasting meant acting before gathering the facts, which showed a lack of judgment. For Ford, that was a red flag against hiring the person.
keyFacts: He watched whether they salted the soup before tasting it
Salting before tasting showed poor judgment, acting without the facts
hints: It isn't about table manners or how fast they eat.
Watch what the candidate does before the first spoonful.
Would you season something you haven't tasted yet?

title: The Roller Coaster Excuse
situation: Two boys come home very late from an amusement park. They tell their father: 'We were on the roller coaster, but as we went down the first hill the engine blew out!' Their father immediately grounds them for lying. How did he know?
solution: Once a roller coaster has gone over the first hill, it does not use an engine at all. It runs on gravity for the rest of the ride. An engine could not have blown out as they went down the first hill, so the father knew the story was made up.
keyFacts: Roller coasters don't use an engine after the first hill
The rest of the ride runs on gravity, so the story is impossible
hints: The lie is in the technical detail of their story.
Think about what makes a roller coaster move once it goes over the top.
After the first climb, nothing is pushing the cars except one natural force.

title: The Slowest Camel Wins
situation: A dying father tells his two sons they must race their camels to a distant city, and the one whose camel arrives last will inherit his fortune. For days the brothers wander slowly, each trying to hold back. Finally they ask a wise man for advice, and afterwards they race to the city as fast as they can. What did he tell them?
solution: The wise man told the brothers to swap camels. The fortune goes to the owner of the camel that arrives last, so each brother now wants the camel he is riding, which belongs to his brother, to get there first. Both race as fast as they can.
keyFacts: The wise man told them to swap camels
The prize goes to the owner of the last camel, not its rider
Each now rides his brother's camel and wants it to arrive first
hints: The rule is about whose camel arrives last, not who arrives last.
Nothing says each brother has to ride his own camel.
If you were on your brother's camel, how fast would you want it to go?

title: Half an Inch Too Tall
situation: A truck driver comes to an overpass and finds his truck is too tall to fit under it. He only needs half an inch. Rather than turn back or take the long way round, he gets a bright idea and drives through. What did he do?
solution: The driver let the air out of the trailer's air bags, its air suspension. With less air in them, the whole truck sat lower. That gave him the half inch he needed to get under the overpass.
keyFacts: He let air out of the trailer's air bags (suspension)
This lowered the truck enough to pass under
hints: He didn't change the bridge or the load. He changed the truck.
Part of the truck is held up by something he can let out.
Think about what would sink a little if you released some air.

title: Mary and Maria at the River
situation: Two sisters, Mary and Maria, had to cross a river. Mary walked across the bridge easily, but Maria jumped into the river and swam across. Afterwards, everyone said Maria was the smarter of the two. Why?
solution: The bridge was old and could only take the weight of a child. Mary was light enough to cross safely, but Maria was too heavy, so she wisely swam across instead of risking the bridge collapsing under her.
keyFacts: The bridge was old and could only take a child's weight
Maria was too heavy for the bridge, so swimming was the safe choice
hints: Mary's easy crossing doesn't mean the bridge was safe for everyone.
Consider the condition of the bridge and how old the sisters are.
What if one sister was much heavier than the other?

title: The Silent Signal at the Diner
situation: Two known robbers are followed by two plain-clothes police officers 24 hours a day. Every morning all four go to the same diner for breakfast. The robbers hang their hats and coats on the cloak-room rack, sit at opposite ends of the counter, eat in silence, put their things back on and leave. They never speak, never pass notes and make no obvious gestures, yet they pass detailed information to each other every day without the police noticing. How?
solution: The robbers use a code built from the cloak-room rack. The first robber picks particular hooks and hangs his clothes in particular ways. The second robber reads the pattern and replies by hanging his own things on other agreed hooks. The officers only see two men hanging up their coats, so they never notice the exchange.
keyFacts: The message is passed through the cloak-room rack
Which hooks they use, and how the hats and coats hang, is a pre-agreed code
The police see only ordinary coat-hanging and miss it
hints: The robbers do something every morning that looks completely ordinary.
Look closely at what happens before they sit down.
Which hooks they pick, and how they hang their coats and hats, carries the message.

title: Why $9.99?
situation: Today we are used to prices like $9.99 or $99.95 rather than neat round numbers like $10 or $100. The custom began in the late 19th and early 20th century, and at first it had nothing to do with making things look cheaper. Why were these odd prices first introduced?
solution: Odd prices were introduced to make the clerk open the cash register and give change on every sale. With a round price, a dishonest clerk could take a customer's whole-dollar note and pocket it without ringing up the sale. Because change was always needed, the clerk had to use the register, which recorded the sale and made a noise, and this deterred theft. The psychological effect on shoppers came later.
keyFacts: The point was to stop theft by clerks
An odd price means the customer needs change
Giving change forces the clerk to open the register, so the sale gets recorded
hints: The trick wasn't aimed at the customer at all.
Think about the person working behind the counter.
If the price is a round number, the clerk doesn't need to open the till to give change.

title: Not a Single Wet Hair
situation: Albert Amblefoot walked outside in a heavy rainstorm for half an hour. He wore no hat, carried no umbrella and held nothing over his head, and his clothes got soaking wet. Yet not a single hair on his head got wet. How could this happen?
solution: Albert is bald. He has no hair on his head, so no hair could get wet.
keyFacts: Albert is bald
He has no hair on his head to get wet
hints: The puzzle never says his head stayed dry.
Pay attention to exactly what stayed dry.
Think about how much hair Albert has.

title: Three Trucks Roll Over Him
situation: A man gets run over by three trucks. Most of the tyres on each truck roll right over him, yet they do not kill him. How is this possible?
solution: The man is down a manhole, underneath the manhole cover. The trucks' tyres roll over the cover above him, and he isn't hurt.
keyFacts: The man is down a manhole
The tyres pass over the manhole cover, not over his body
hints: The tyres never actually touch him.
Think about what could be between the man and the road.
He is below the road surface.

title: The Postman and the Dog
situation: A postman has to deliver a letter to a house surrounded by a five-foot wall. The only way to reach the house is along the main path, and a ferocious dog is tied by a long lead to a nearby tree, so the whole path is within its reach. If the postman walks up the path, the dog is sure to attack him. How does he outwit the dog and deliver the letter?
solution: The postman doesn't use the path at all. He throws the letter over the wall. The dog is tied to the tree and can't reach him there.
keyFacts: The postman avoids the path
He throws the letter over the wall
The dog is tied up and can't reach him at the wall
hints: Does the postman have to walk up to the front door?
The wall is only five feet high.
The letter can reach the house even if the postman doesn't.

title: Two Deaths and a Trip Home
situation: A girl killed two people. She never faced any consequences. The only thing that happened to her was that she got to go home. What is her name?
solution: Her name is Dorothy, from The Wizard of Oz. Her house landed on the Wicked Witch of the East and she melted the Wicked Witch of the West with water, and in the end she got to go home.
keyFacts: The girl is Dorothy
She is from The Wizard of Oz
hints: She isn't a real person.
It's a famous story in which the heroine just wants to go home.
Think of witches, ruby slippers and 'There's no place like home.'

title: Home by Eight
situation: A man phones his wife from work and tells her he won't be home until eight o'clock. He gets home at two minutes past eight, and his wife is furious with him. Why?
solution: He never said whether he meant 8 in the evening or 8 in the morning. He came home at 8:02 the next morning, after being out all night.
keyFacts: He didn't say AM or PM
He got home at 8 in the morning, not 8 in the evening
He had been away all night
hints: Two minutes late isn't the problem.
There are two eight o'clocks in every day.
Which eight o'clock did he actually get home at?

title: The Logic-Loving Cannibals
situation: While hiking in a remote jungle, you are caught by cannibals who love logic. They let you make one statement: if it is true, they will burn you, and if it is false, they will boil you in oil. What can you say to escape?
solution: You say: 'You will boil me in oil.' If that is true, they must burn you, which makes it false. If it is false, they must boil you in oil, which makes it true. The cannibals can't carry out either punishment without breaking their own rule, so they have to let you go.
keyFacts: You say 'You will boil me in oil'
The statement creates a paradox under their rules
Neither punishment can be carried out, so you go free
hints: The cannibals keep their own rules strictly.
Make a statement about what they will do to you.
Pick the statement that becomes false if they carry out the punishment it names.

title: The Dog That Stayed Dry
situation: A dog is on one side of a lake and its owner is on the other. The owner calls the dog, and it crosses the lake without getting wet. How?
solution: The water was frozen, so the dog simply walked across the ice.
keyFacts: The lake was frozen
The dog walked across on the ice
hints: The dog didn't go around the lake.
Think about the season.
Water isn't always liquid.

title: Who Wrote on the Wall?
situation: A student at school wrote something rude on the wall, and nobody owned up to it. Without a confession or a witness, the teacher still worked out who did it. How?
solution: The teacher had every student write a sentence on the board. One student's handwriting matched the writing on the wall, and that showed who had done it.
keyFacts: The teacher had every student write something
The culprit was found by matching handwriting
hints: The culprit gave himself away without meaning to.
Everyone was asked to do the same simple task.
Compare how each student writes.

title: Six Eggs, One Left
situation: There are six eggs in a basket. Six people each take one of the eggs. Yet one egg is still left in the basket. How can that be?
solution: The last person took the basket along with the last egg, which was still inside it. Everyone got one egg each, and there is still one egg in the basket.
keyFacts: The last person took the whole basket
The last egg was still inside the basket when it was taken
hints: Think about how each person took their egg.
Did everyone have to take their egg out of the basket?
One person took something more than just an egg.

title: Same Speed, Different Arrival
situation: Two cars drive from point A to point B. They travel at exactly the same speed along exactly the same route, so the trip takes each of them exactly the same time. Yet one car arrives about 34.73 minutes after the other. How is that possible?
solution: One car simply left point A 34.73 minutes earlier than the other. Both trips take the same time, but because they started at different times they also arrive at different times.
keyFacts: The cars did not leave at the same time
One car left 34.73 minutes earlier
hints: Nothing unusual happens on the road.
The puzzle tells you how long the trip takes, but not when it begins.
Ask yourself whether they both started at the same moment.

title: Regret at the 23rd Storey
situation: A woman jumps off a 33-storey building. As she falls past the 23rd storey, she immediately regrets her decision. What is going on?
solution: She is bungee jumping from the 24th storey of the 33-storey building. As she passes the 23rd storey, just after jumping, she gets scared and wishes she hadn't done it, but she is tied to a bungee cord and is safe.
keyFacts: She is bungee jumping
She jumped from the 24th storey, so she has only just jumped
She is attached to a cord and is not in danger
hints: She is not trying to hurt herself.
She did not jump from the roof: the 23rd storey comes right after she jumps.
She is tied to something stretchy.

title: Younger Five Years On
situation: Kiran was 20 years old in the year 1980. In the year 1985, he was only 15 years old. How come?
solution: The years are B.C. Kiran was born in 2000 B.C., so in 1980 B.C. he was 20 years old, and in 1985 B.C. he was 15. Before Christ, the year numbers count down as time moves forward, so 1985 B.C. came five years before 1980 B.C.
keyFacts: The years are B.C.
He was born in 2000 B.C.
B.C. year numbers get smaller as time passes, so 1985 B.C. came before 1980 B.C.
hints: Nothing is wrong with Kiran or with his records.
Kiran lived a very, very long time ago.
Think about which way the year numbers count before year 1.

title: Two Fathers, Two Sons, Two Apples
situation: There are two sons and two fathers. The first father gives two apples to his son, and the other father gives two apples to his son. Yet there are only two apples altogether. How can that be?
solution: There are only three people: a grandfather, a father and a son. The middle man is both a son (of the grandfather) and a father (of the boy), so two fathers and two sons are only three people. The grandfather gives two apples to his son, who hands the same two apples on to his own son.
keyFacts: There are only three people: grandfather, father and son
The middle man counts as both a father and a son
The same two apples are passed down
hints: Count the people, not the roles.
One person could be described in two ways.
Think of three generations of one family.

title: An Extraordinary Moment in 1978
situation: Something very extraordinary happened on the 6th of May, 1978, at 12:34 a.m. What was it?
solution: Nothing happened in the world itself; it was about the numbers. Written as a time and date, the moment was 12:34 on 5/6/78, and the digits run in order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.
keyFacts: It is about how the time and date are written
12:34 5/6/78 gives the digits 1 to 8 in order
hints: It isn't a historical event.
Write the time and the date down next to each other.
Write the date as month/day/year.

title: Robbed, Then Arrested
situation: Three men rob a house and get away with hundreds of thousands of euros. Yet it is the owner of the house who gets arrested. Why?
solution: The owner of the house was an accomplice of the robbers. He was in on the robbery, so it was the owner the police arrested.
keyFacts: The owner was an accomplice of the robbers
The robbery was an inside job
hints: The owner is not as innocent as he seems.
Did the owner know about the robbery beforehand?
The owner and the three men were working together.

title: The Sleepover Spider
situation: Five girls are at a sleepover. One of them yells, 'There's a spider on the wall!' and the others all scream, 'Kill it!' Yet the spider gets away alive. How?
solution: They all yelled for somebody to kill it, but nobody actually did. The girls were all too scared of the spider to go near it, so it escaped.
keyFacts: Nobody actually tried to kill the spider
The girls were too afraid of it
hints: Shouting 'kill it' is not the same as doing it.
Think about how the girls feel about spiders.
None of them was brave enough to go near it.

title: Five Litres in a Three-Litre Pot
situation: In a skills test, a teacher gives a student an open pot that can hold only 3 litres of water. He tells the student to bring 5 litres of water from the market. How can the student bring 5 litres of water in a pot that only holds 3 litres?
solution: He makes two trips. First he fills the pot to the brim and brings those 3 litres to the teacher. Then he goes back, fills the pot two-thirds full and brings the other 2 litres, making 5 litres in all.
keyFacts: He makes more than one trip
3 litres on the first trip and 2 litres on the second

title: Two Women on the Balcony
